catalog_quote: Sahaptin contains many of the classic properties of accentual systems (McCawley 1978): unpredictable location of accent within morphemes, a contrast between accented vs. unaccented morphemes, and a culminativity principle. In addition, high pitch is a phonetic correlate of accent (Hargus and Beavert to appear), as is often the case in such systems. All Sahaptin data in this article come from the second author, who is a native speaker of the Yakima dialect. ... Yakima Sahaptin roots vary in length, with most roots one to three syllables long. In roots, accent (transcribed here with acute accent) can fall on any syllable: [ánut’at] ‘orphan’, [talámat] ‘pipe’, [anahúj] ‘black bear’. ... As noted by Jacobs 1931, there is a contrast between accented and unaccented affixes in Sahaptin. Jacobs gives [páwat’ana] ‘he struck at him’, with [pá]- inverse ... vs. [pa]- 3pl.nom. sources.quote: Yakima: 'every lexical word must have an accent... Although roots must have an accent, its location is unpredictable... affixes are either accented or not... accent shifts from root to (outermost) affix obligatorily... except for a small set of strong roots' (p. 2). sources.quote: 'The prosodic system of Sahaptin fits the characteristics of what is usually described as pitch accent... Sahaptin morphemes are either underlyingly accented or unaccented... Words surface with one accent... if a word contains both an accented prefix and an accented root, the accent surfaces only on the prefix... If a word contains both an accented suffix and an accented root, the strongest accent in the word is on the suffix'; 'Minimal pairs for accent location can also be found in polysyllabic, monomorphemic roots: pámta / pamtá ...'; 'principal phonetic correlates of accent are increased pi

sources.quote: 'Ichishkiin has word level stress, with one primary stress per spoken word. Stress is indicated with raised pitch and greater intensity in the stressed syllable (Hargus and Beavert 2005)... a stress shift can change the meaning of a word' (p. 52); 'Where the stress will fall in a root is not predictable. Any syllable of a root can be stressed' (p. 53); stress-stealing affixes; 'stress-stealing suffix > strong root > stress-stealing prefix > root' (p. 56); 'Stress also varies by dialect... Because the Yakama area includes speakers of a number of dialects, you may hear different stress patterns
